facts.statement: Oohkotokia was a large, heavily built, four-legged herbivore reaching up to 5 meters in length and weighing up to 2 metric tons.
facts.quote: It was a large, heavily built, quadrupedal, herbivore, that could grow up to 5 m long and weigh up to 2 MT.

facts.statement: The skull of Oohkotokia is similar to those of Euoplocephalus but is distinguished by a relatively smooth overall surface texture compared to other ankylosaurids of the same era.
facts.quote: The skull of this genus bears great similarity to skulls that have been referred to Euoplocephalus, but is significant because it has a relatively smooth overall surface texture when compared to the skulls of most other ankylosaurids from the same time period.

facts.statement: Oohkotokia possessed a tail club made of bone plates permeated with soft tissue capable of absorbing thousands of pounds of force.
facts.quote: Its tail club was made of several plates of bone, permeated by soft tissue, which allowed the absorption of thousands of pounds of force.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the large tail clubs of Oohkotokia may have been used for self-defense against predators or rivals, or for sexual selection.
facts.quote: The large clubs at the end of their tails may have been used in self-defense, by swinging the club at predators or rivals, or in sexual selection.

facts.statement: The genus Oohkotokia contains the single type species Oohkotokia horneri, which was named and described in 2013 by Paul Penkalski.
facts.quote: Oohkotokia contains a single type species, Oohkotokia horneri, named and described in 2013 by Paul Penkalski.

facts.statement: Paul Penkalski described the genus Oohkotokia after rediscovering a specimen in the collection of Montana's Museum of the Rockies that had been stored for over three decades.
facts.quote: Penkalski described this genus after finding it in the collection of Montana's Museum of the Rockies where it had been stored for more than three decades.

facts.statement: The name Oohkotokia means "child of stone" in reference to the dinosaur's extensive body armor, derived from a Blackfoot word and a Latin suffix.
facts.quote: The generic name, Oohkotokia, is derived from the Blackfoot animate noun "ooh'kotoka", meaning "large stone" and the Latin suffix "ia" meaning "derived from"; thus "child of stone", which is a reference to its extensive body armor.

facts.statement: Oohkotokia fossils are known from the upper levels of the Two Medicine Formation in Montana, dating to about 74 million years ago during the late Campanian stage.
facts.quote: It is known from the upper levels of the Two Medicine Formation (late Campanian stage, about 74 Ma ago) of Montana, United States.

facts.statement: Radiometric dating of the Two Medicine Formation where Oohkotokia remains were found indicates an age of approximately 74 million years.
facts.quote: The remains of Oohkotokia, MOR 433 were recovered in the Upper Member of the Two Medicine Formation, in Montana, which radiometric dating has shown to be approximately 74 million years old.

facts.statement: Studies suggest Oohkotokia lived in a seasonal, semi-arid environment with possible rainshadows from the Cordilleran highlands.
facts.quote: Studies suggest that the paleoenvironment of the Two Medicine Formation featured a seasonal, semi-arid climate with possible rainshadows from the Cordilleran highlands.

facts.statement: Oohkotokia is classified as a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur belonging to the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.
facts.quote: Oohkotokia ( ) is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur within the subfamily Ankylosaurinae.

facts.statement: Paul Penkalski assigned Oohkotokia to the subfamily Ankylosaurinae based on skull anatomy and body armor morphology.
facts.quote: Penkalski (2013) assigned this genus to Ankylosaurinae based on anatomical features present in the skull and the morphology of its body armor.

facts.statement: Oohkotokia shared its habitat with diverse fauna including oviraptorosaurs, ornithopods, nodosaurs, ceratopsians, Troodon, dromaeosaurids, and tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: The Two Medicine Formation has produced the remains of oviraptorosaurs, ornithopods, the nodosaur Edmontonia, the ceratopsians Achelousaurus, Brachyceratops, Cerasinops, and Einiosaurus among others, Troodon, the dromaeosaurids Bambiraptor, Dromaeosaurus and Saurornitholestes, and the tyrannosauroids Albertosaurus, Daspletosaurus and Gorgosaurus.

facts.statement: A partial skull once referred to Dyoplosaurus but now associated with Oohkotokia features very large squamosal horns and unique Z-shaped tooth carinae.
facts.quote: Specimen USNM 11892, a partial skull with five teeth first described and referred to Dyoplosaurus by Gilmore in 1930. This specimen has very large squamosal horns and teeth with shelf-like labial cingula and unique Z-shaped carinae in occlusal view.

facts.statement: The crushed condition of the Oohkotokia skull suggests it was damaged by dinoturbation, the trampling of bones by passing dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The crushing suggests that it was the result of dinoturbation, which is the trampling of soils, sediments and bones by passing dinosaurs.
